sections.title: Why this module matters
sections.body: Functions in Go are first-class values, and interviewers test that you understand what that means in practice. Multiple return values, closures, defer, and the loop-variable capture gotcha all appear in fresher interviews because they catch people who learned Go syntax but not Go idioms. Understanding defer and panic/recover is also essential for reading any real Go codebase.

sections.title: Mental model
sections.body:
Three things to remember:

- **Functions are values.** You can assign `func(x int) int { return x * 2 }` to a variable, pass it to another function, or return it — just like Python lambdas but with full syntax. This is the foundation for closures, callbacks, and middleware patterns.
- **Multiple returns replace exceptions for expected errors.** Instead of throwing a `FileNotFoundException` (Java) or raising an `IOError` (Python), Go functions return `(result, error)`. The caller decides what to do — no stack unwinding, no hidden control flow.
- **`defer` runs LIFO at return, but arguments are evaluated immediately.** Think of `defer f(x)` as 'capture the value of x now, call f(x) when this function returns'. This is the most common interview trick question on defer.

sections.title: Must-know concepts
sections.body:
- **Function signatures** — `func name(param type) returnType`; functions are first-class values assignable to variables of type `func(...)`
- **Multiple return values** — `func divide(a, b float64) (float64, error)` returns both result and error; caller checks `if err != nil`
- **Named return values** — named returns declare variables in the signature; `return` with no arguments returns them (naked return); useful in short functions, confusing in long ones
- **Closures and captured variables** — a function literal captures variables from its enclosing scope by reference, not by value; the classic loop-capture bug: `go func() { fmt.Println(i) }()` inside a loop captures the loop variable `i`, not its current value
- **Variadic functions** — `func sum(nums ...int)` accepts zero or more ints; spread a slice with `sum(mySlice...)`
- **Defer basics** — deferred calls execute LIFO when the function returns; `defer f.Close()` immediately after opening a file is the safe pattern
- **Panic and recover basics** — `panic(msg)` halts normal execution and unwinds the stack; `recover()` inside a deferred function catches the panic; use only for truly unrecoverable states, not normal errors

sections.title: Likely interview hooks
sections.body:
- **Loop variable capture in closures** — `for i := 0; i < 3; i++ { go func() { fmt.Println(i) }() }` prints `3 3 3`, not `0 1 2`. The fix: pass `i` as a function argument — `go func(i int) { fmt.Println(i) }(i)`. This is one of the most common Go fresher gotchas.
- **Defer argument evaluation timing** — in `defer fmt.Println(x)`, the value of `x` is captured at the defer statement, not at function return. This trips up candidates who think defer is like `finally`.
- **Named returns and naked return** — naked `return` can return stale values if the named variable was modified after the deferred function. Interviewers ask: 'what does this function return?' pointing at a function with both defer and named returns.
- **Panic is not an exception** — `panic` should not be used for expected errors like 'user not found'. The correct pattern is returning an error value. Panics are for invariant violations — things that should never happen.

sections.title: Speaking template
sections.body: > *"In Go, functions are first-class values and the idiomatic error-handling pattern is to return a result and an error together — the caller checks `if err != nil`. Closures capture variables by reference, which means a loop variable captured by a goroutine closure will hold the final loop value unless you pass it as an argument. `defer` executes LIFO at function return with arguments evaluated at the defer statement — which is why `defer f.Close()` is the standard safe-close pattern."*
